nameStory: The Bordered Wedge-shaped Beetle gets its name from its distinctive triangular body shape that tapers like a wedge from front to back. The 'bordered' part refers to the contrasting edges on its wing covers (elytra), which create a framed appearance that helps distinguish it from other small beetles.
description: This small, wedge-shaped beetle is a fascinating summer visitor to New England flowers. Adults have an elongated, triangular body that narrows toward the rear, with wing covers that extend beyond the tip of their abdomen and spread apart at the ends. They're most noticeable for their unusually long mouthparts, which they use like a straw to sip nectar from flowers. Despite their delicate appearance, these beetles have a complex life cycle involving parasitism of wasp larvae.

idTips.label: Wedge-shaped body
idTips.description: The body tapers dramatically from head to tail like a triangle, creating an unmistakable wedge silhouette that no other common flower beetle shares

idTips.label: Prolonged mouthparts
idTips.description: Long, straw-like mouthparts extend noticeably forward from the head, giving them an almost hummingbird-like appearance as they probe deep into flowers

idTips.label: Spreading wing covers
idTips.description: The hard wing covers (elytra) don't meet at the back but instead diverge and spread apart at the tips, revealing a gap that shows the darker body underneath

idTips.label: Male antennae
idTips.description: Males have feathery, comb-like antennae that feel delicate to the touch, while females have more simply serrated (saw-toothed) antennae

idTips.label: Flower-visiting behavior
idTips.description: Often seen actively feeding on elderberry clusters and goldenrod blooms, moving deliberately from flower to flower rather than flying away when approached

habitat: Look for these beetles on flowering plants in open areas like meadows, field edges, and woodland clearings throughout New England. They're particularly drawn to elderberry bushes and goldenrod patches in late summer, often in areas where native ground-nesting wasps are also active. You'll find them in both rural and suburban settings wherever their preferred flowers bloom.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. The larval stages are developing as parasites inside wasp nests from the previous year's cycle.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults emerge and can be found actively feeding on flowers. This is the best time to spot them on elderberries and early goldenrod blooms.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue visiting late-season goldenrod and other flowers. Females are laying eggs on flower petals during this time, preparing for next year's generation.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. The species overwinters in larval form inside their wasp host nests, waiting for spring development.

funFact: The tiny larvae of this beetle are master hitchhikers — they wait on flower petals until an unsuspecting wasp visits, then climb aboard for a free ride back to the wasp's nest where they become uninvited houseguests, eating the wasp babies' food stores!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with small longhorn beetles, but the wedge shape and spreading wing tips are distinctive. Remember: if it looks like a tiny triangle with a straw for a mouth on your goldenrod, it's likely this species.
contextualKnowledge: The family name 'Ripiphoridae' comes from Greek meaning 'fan-bearer,' referring to the males' feathery antennae. Despite being called 'wedge-shaped beetles,' they're more closely related to blister beetles than to typical beetles, reflecting their unusual parasitic lifestyle.
compareHints: This is the only Macrosiagon species recorded in New England, making identification easier within its genus. Compared to other wedge-shaped beetles in the family, the Bordered Wedge-shaped Beetle is distinguished by its specific host relationships with crabronid wasps and its preference for elderberry and goldenrod flowers. Other ripiphorid beetles in the region tend to be associated with different host insects and flower preferences.
